Recall: Two Balance Principles for the Buck

  • Three ingredients: the small ripple approximation, the inductor over one period, and steady state (\(i_{L}\) repeats every \(T_{s}\)).
  • Volt-second balance: \(\langle v_{L} \rangle_{T_{s}} = 0\) in steady state \(\Rightarrow V = DV_{g}\), so \(M(D) = D\).
  • Charge balance: \(\langle i_{C} \rangle_{T_{s}} = 0\) in steady state \(\Rightarrow I_{L} = V/R\).
  • Current ripple: a linear ramp, \(\Delta i_{L} = DT_{s}\left(V_{g}-V\right)/L\); peak \(I_{L} + \Delta i_{L}/2\).

Today: the ripple revisited, the same principles on a boost, and a diode in place of a switch.

Additional Notes on Peak-to-Peak Current

Last lecture we derived \(\;\Delta i_{L}=\dfrac{DT_{s}\left(V_{g}-V\right)}{L}\)

  • The load varies, and the average inductor current follows it: for the buck \(I_{L} = I_{o} = V/R\), so \(I_{L} \in [I_{L,min},\,I_{L,max}]\) as \(R\) ranges over \([R_{max},\,R_{min}]\), with \(I_{L,max} = V/R_{min}\)
  • Typically, \(\Delta i_{L}\) is designed to be 20% to 40% of the maximum average inductor current, \(I_{L,max}\)

Additional Notes on Peak-to-Peak Current

  • Let’s say that we want to limit \(\Delta i_{L}\) to \(X\%\) of \(I_{L,max}\)
    • e.g. \(X = 20\%\) or \(40\%\)
  • Let’s find an expression for the minimum inductance required to ensure this.

Recall:

\[ \Delta i_{L}=\frac{DT_{s}\left(V_{g}-V\right)}{L} \]

With \(\Delta i_{L}=(X/100\%)\,V/R_{min}\) (and \(D=V/V_{g}\), \(T_{s}=1/f_{s}\)), re-arranging:

\[ L>\frac{R_{min}\left(V_{g}-V\right)}{V_{g}f_{s}\,(X/100\%)} \]

Another Two-Switch DC-DC Converter: the Boost Converter

  • A buck converter is for stepping down a voltage (i.e. output voltage < input voltage)
  • A boost converter is for stepping up a voltage (i.e. output voltage > input voltage)

Two Operating States

\(v_{L}=v_{g}\)
\(i_{C}=-\dfrac{v}{R}\)
SRA: \(\;v_{L}=V_{g},\qquad i_{C}=-\dfrac{V}{R}\)

\(v_{L}=v_{g}-v\)
\(i_{C}=i_{L}-\dfrac{v}{R}\)
SRA: \(\;v_{L}=V_{g}-V,\qquad i_{C}=I_{L}-\dfrac{V}{R}\)

Inductor Volt-Second Balance: Solving for V

We know:
① \(0 \le t < DT_{s}\): \(\;v_{L}=V_{g}\)
② \(DT_{s} \le t < T_{s}\): \(\;v_{L}=V_{g}-V\)
with \(D' \equiv 1-D\) (② lasts \(D'T_{s}\))

\(\displaystyle \langle v_{L} \rangle_{T_{s}} = \frac{1}{T_{s}} \int_{0}^{T_{s}} v_{L}\,dt = 0\)

\(\displaystyle \phantom{\langle v_{L} \rangle_{T_{s}}} = \frac{1}{T_{s}}\left[V_{g}\,DT_{s} + \left(V_{g}-V\right)D'T_{s}\right]\)

\(\displaystyle \phantom{\langle v_{L} \rangle_{T_{s}}} = V_{g}D + V_{g}D' - VD' = V_{g} - VD'\)

\(\displaystyle \Rightarrow V=\frac{V_{g}}{D'}\)

Conversion Ratio of the Converter, M(D)

\[M(D)=\frac{V}{V_{g}}\]

\[\phantom{M(D)}=\frac{1}{D'}=\frac{1}{1-D}\]

Question: what might a practical converter’s ratio look like as \(D \to 1\)?

Charge Balance: Solving for the Inductor Current

We know:
① \(0 \le t < DT_{s}\): \(\;i_{C}=-V/R\)
② \(DT_{s} \le t < T_{s}\): \(\;i_{C}=I_{L}-V/R\)

\(\displaystyle \langle i_{C} \rangle_{T_{s}} = \frac{1}{T_{s}} \int_{0}^{T_{s}} i_{C}\,dt = 0\)

\(\displaystyle \phantom{\langle i_{C} \rangle_{T_{s}}} = \frac{1}{T_{s}}\left[-\frac{V}{R}\,DT_{s} + \left(I_{L}-\frac{V}{R}\right)D'T_{s}\right]\)

\(\displaystyle \phantom{\langle i_{C} \rangle_{T_{s}}} = -\frac{V}{R} + I_{L}D'\)

\(\displaystyle \Rightarrow I_{L}=\frac{V}{RD'} = \frac{V^{2}}{RV_{g}}\) (since \(D'=V_{g}/V\))

Sizing L for the Boost Converter

Requirement: \(\Delta i_{L}<(X/100\%)\,I_{L,max}\)

We know:
① \(0 \le t < DT_{s}\): \(\;v_{L}=V_{g}\)
② \(DT_{s} \le t < T_{s}\): \(\;v_{L}=V_{g}-V\)

\(\displaystyle \Delta i_{L} = \frac{1}{L}\int_{0}^{DT_{s}} v_{L}\,dt\)

\(\displaystyle \phantom{\Delta i_{L}} = \frac{V_{g}DT_{s}}{L}\)

Subbing in \(\Delta i_{L}=(X/100\%)\,I_{L,max}\) (where \(I_{L,max}=V/(R_{min}D')\) for the boost), \(D = 1-V_{g}/V\) and \(T_{s}=1/f_{s}\), then re-arranging for \(L\) yields:

\(\displaystyle L>\frac{V_{g}\left(1-V_{g}/V\right)}{f_{s}\,(X/100\%)\,I_{L,max}}\)

Sizing C for the Boost Converter

Requirement: \(\Delta v_{C}<(X/100\%)\,V\)

We know:
① \(0 \le t < DT_{s}\): \(\;i_{C}=-V/R\)
② \(DT_{s} \le t < T_{s}\): \(\;i_{C}=I_{L}-V/R\)

\(\displaystyle \Delta v_{C} = -\frac{1}{C}\int_{0}^{DT_{s}} i_{C}\,dt\)

\(\displaystyle \phantom{\Delta v_{C}} = -\frac{1}{C}\left(-\frac{V}{R}\right)DT_{s} = \frac{V\,DT_{s}}{RC}\)

Subbing in \(\Delta v_{C}=(X/100\%)\,V\), \(D = 1-V_{g}/V\) and \(T_{s}=1/f_{s}\), then re-arranging for \(C\) yields:

\(\displaystyle C>\frac{V-V_{g}}{R\,f_{s}\,(X/100\%)\,V}\)

Back to the Buck Converter

  • With \(L\) and \(C\) both sized for the boost, we return to the buck converter to size its capacitor.
  • The method that worked for the boost needs one adjustment here. Let’s see why.

Challenge for the Buck Converter

  • Over the whole period \(0 \to T_{s}\), KCL at the output node gives \(\;i_{C} = i_{L} - v/R\).
  • Apply the small ripple approximation to both \(i_{L}\) and \(v\): \(\;i_{C} = I_{L} - V/R\)
  • But for the buck, \(I_{L} = V/R\), so this predicts \(\;i_{C} = 0\) and a perfectly flat \(v = V\).
  • The real converter disagrees: \(i_{C}\) swings about zero and \(v\) ripples about \(V\). The approximation threw away exactly what we need to size \(C\).

Do Not Apply the SRA to the Inductor Current

We know: \(\;i_{C}=i_{L}-\dfrac{v}{R}\)

  • Both terms contribute ripple to \(i_{C}\): \(\Delta i_{L}\) from the inductor and \(\Delta v/R\) from the load. A typical design allows \(\Delta i_{L}\) of 20-40% of \(I_{L}\) but \(\Delta v\) of only about 1% of \(V\), and since \(I_{L} = V/R\), \(\Delta v/R \approx 0.01\,I_{L}\). The inductor contributes 20 to 40 times more ripple to \(i_{C}\) than the load does, so dropping \(\Delta v\) is a reasonable approximation; dropping \(\Delta i_{L}\) would remove almost all of \(i_{C}\).
  • So apply the SRA to \(v\) only, \(v \approx V\): \(\quad i_{C}=i_{L}-V/R\)
  • And \(V/R\) is known: charge balance gave \(I_{L} = V/R\), so \(i_{C} = i_{L} - I_{L}\) is the ripple of \(i_{L}\) alone, a triangle centred on zero.

From Capacitor Current to Output Ripple

\(\displaystyle i_{C} = C\,\frac{dv}{dt}\) \(\displaystyle \;\Rightarrow\; v(t_{2}) - v(t_{1}) = \frac{1}{C}\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} i_{C}\,dt = \frac{\Delta Q}{C}\)
\(\displaystyle \;\Rightarrow\;\) from minimum to maximum of \(v\): \(\;\displaystyle \Delta v_{C} = \frac{\Delta Q}{C}\)

  • \(v\) rises while \(i_{C} > 0\) and falls while \(i_{C} < 0\): maximum at the downward zero crossing of \(i_{C}\), minimum at the upward one.
  • Between those instants \(i_{C} > 0\), so \(\Delta Q\) is the charge in the positive lobe of \(i_{C}\) and \(\Delta v_{C}\) the peak-to-peak ripple.

So we need two things: the instants where \(i_{C}\) crosses zero, which bound the lobe, and the charge \(\Delta Q = \int i_{C}\,dt\) between them.

Where the Triangle Crosses Zero

  • Recall from Lecture 2: each ramp of \(i_{L}\) is linear, so \(I_{L}\) is the midpoint of \(I_{min}\) and \(I_{max}\) and the peak sits \(\Delta i_{L}/2\) above \(I_{L}\), for any \(D\).
  • \(i_{C} = i_{L} - I_{L}\) therefore swings between \(\pm\Delta i_{L}/2\) and crosses zero at the midpoint of each ramp: at \(t_{1} = DT_{s}/2\) on the rise, at \(t_{2} = DT_{s} + D'T_{s}/2\) on the fall.
  • The positive lobe is a triangle of height \(\Delta i_{L}/2\) on a base of

\[ \left(DT_{s} + \tfrac{1}{2}D'T_{s}\right) - \tfrac{1}{2}DT_{s} = \tfrac{1}{2}(D + D')\,T_{s} = \frac{T_{s}}{2} \]

Sizing C for the Buck Converter

Requirement: \(\Delta v_{C}<(X/100\%)\,V\)

We know: \(\;i_{C} = i_{L} - I_{L}\) crosses zero at \(t_{1} = DT_{s}/2\) and \(t_{2} = DT_{s} + D'T_{s}/2\): a triangle of height \(\Delta i_{L}/2\) on a base \(T_{s}/2\)

\(\displaystyle \Delta Q = \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} i_{C}\,dt = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{T_{s}}{2}\right)\frac{\Delta i_{L}}{2} = \frac{\Delta i_{L}\,T_{s}}{8}\)

\(\displaystyle \Delta Q = C\left[v(t_{2}) - v(t_{1})\right] = C\,\Delta v_{C} \;\Rightarrow\; \Delta v_{C} = \frac{\Delta i_{L}}{8\,Cf_{s}}\)

Subbing in \(\Delta v_{C}=(X/100\%)\,V\) and \(\Delta i_{L}=V\left(V_{g}-V\right)/\left(V_{g}Lf_{s}\right)\), then re-arranging for \(C\) yields:

\(\displaystyle C>\frac{V_{g}-V}{8\,V_{g}Lf_{s}^{2}\,(X/100\%)}\)

Practical Realization

Until now, we’ve been considering ideal switches:

A real switch is a semiconductor device. What do we build switches 1 and 2 from?

Two Ways to Implement the Buck’s Switches

  1. One active switch (a MOSFET, or an IGBT with an anti-parallel diode) plus one diode: the diode buck

  2. Two active switches: the synchronous buck

We analyze a). The diode has no gate: it is turned on and off by the external circuit, not by a controller.

The Diode Buck in Continuous Conduction Mode

Continuous conduction mode (CCM): \(i_{L}>0\) throughout the switching period.

The diode carries \(i_{L}\) whenever \(Q_{1}\) is off (the red loop), but a diode conducts in one direction only: it cannot carry a negative \(i_{L}\).

Only the Average Current Follows the Load

From before, we know that: \(\;i_{L}(0)=I_{L}-\Delta i_{L}/2\), \(\;i_{L}(DT_{s})=I_{L}+\Delta i_{L}/2\)

Additionally, it is important to note that:
\(I_{L}\) is load (i.e. \(R\)) dependent: \(\;I_{L}=V/R\)
\(\Delta i_{L}\) is not load dependent: \(\;\Delta i_{L}=\dfrac{V\left(V_{g}-V\right)}{V_{g}Lf_{s}}\)

So as the load lightens (\(R\) rises), \(I_{L}\) falls while the ripple stays put. What happens when \(I_{L}\) reaches \(\Delta i_{L}/2\)?

Boundary Conduction Mode

Let’s look at the case when \(I_{L}=\Delta i_{L}/2\)

Boundary conduction mode (BCM): \(i_{L}\) just reaches zero at the end of the switching period, at the instant \(Q_{1}\) turns on again.

Discontinuous Conduction Mode

Let’s look at the case when \(I_{L}<\Delta i_{L}/2\)

Discontinuous conduction mode (DCM): for some duration of each switching period (i.e. \(D_{3}T_{s}\neq 0\)), the inductor current is equal to 0.

Once \(i_{L}\) reaches zero the diode turns off. With \(Q_{1}\) also off, nothing can drive \(i_{L}\), so it stays at zero for the rest of the period: a third interval, \(D_{3}T_{s}\).

The Road to the Conversion Ratio in DCM

The rest of the lecture derives the conversion ratio in DCM. Four steps:

  1. Three intervals, not two – \(Q_{1}\) on; the diode on; then both off with \(i_{L} = 0\), so \(v_{L} = 0\).
  2. Inductor volt-second balance – gives \(M\) in terms of \(D\) and a second, unknown, duty ratio \(D_{2}\).
  3. A second equation for \(I_{L}\) – capacitor charge balance and the triangular waveshape of \(i_{L}\) together fix \(D_{2}\).
  4. Combine – \(M = V/V_{g}\) in known quantities: \(D\), \(L\), \(R\) and \(T_{s}\).

DCM: Three Operating States

① \(0 \le t < DT_{s}\): \(Q_{1}\) on
\(v_{L}=v_{g}-v\)
\(i_{C}=i_{L}-v/R\)

② \(DT_{s} \le t < (D+D_{2})T_{s}\): diode on
\(v_{L}=-v\)
\(i_{C}=i_{L}-v/R\)

③ \((D+D_{2})T_{s} \le t < T_{s}\): both off
\(v_{L}=0\) (since \(i_{L}=0\))
\(i_{C}=i_{L}-v/R\)

Volt-Second Balance in DCM

With the SRA (\(v \approx V\), \(v_{g} \approx V_{g}\)) on each interval:

\(\displaystyle \langle v_{L} \rangle_{T_{s}} = \frac{1}{T_{s}}\int_{0}^{T_{s}} v_{L}\,dt = 0\)

\(\displaystyle \phantom{\langle v_{L} \rangle_{T_{s}}} = \frac{1}{T_{s}}\left[\left(V_{g}-V\right)DT_{s} + \left(-V\right)D_{2}T_{s} + 0 \cdot D_{3}T_{s}\right] = \left(V_{g}-V\right)D - VD_{2}\)

Solving for the conversion ratio: \(\;\displaystyle M = \frac{V}{V_{g}} = \frac{D}{D+D_{2}}\)

Problem: volt-second balance and capacitor charge balance give us only two equations, but DCM brings a third unknown, \(D_{2}\), along with \(V\) and \(I_{L}\). We need one more expression to write \(M\) in known quantities.

Two Expressions for the Inductor Current

To find \(D_{2}\) we write \(I_{L}\) two ways and equate them:

  • First, from capacitor charge balance, as before

\[\langle i_{C} \rangle_{T_{s}} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; I_{L} = \frac{V}{R}\]

  • Second, from the waveshape of \(i_{L}\), which is where \(D_{2}\) enters

The Waveshape of the Inductor Current

On ①, \(0 \le t < DT_{s}\): \(\;v_{L}=V_{g}-V\)

Average: the triangle’s area, base \(\left(D+D_{2}\right)T_{s}\), height \(\Delta i_{L}\)

\(\displaystyle \langle i_{L} \rangle_{T_{s}} = \frac{1}{T_{s}}\int_{0}^{T_{s}} i_{L}\,dt = \frac{1}{T_{s}}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\left(D+D_{2}\right)T_{s}\,\Delta i_{L}\)

\(\displaystyle \phantom{\langle i_{L} \rangle_{T_{s}}} = \frac{1}{2}\left(D+D_{2}\right)\Delta i_{L} \qquad (1)\)

Peak: the rise of \(i_{L}\) over interval ①

\(\displaystyle \Delta i_{L} = \frac{1}{L}\int_{0}^{DT_{s}} v_{L}\,dt = \frac{\left(V_{g}-V\right)DT_{s}}{L} \qquad (2)\)

Combine: (2) in (1): \(I_{L}\) a second way, with \(D_{2}\) in it

\(\displaystyle I_{L} = \langle i_{L} \rangle_{T_{s}} = \left(V_{g}-V\right)\left(\frac{DT_{s}}{2L}\right)\left(D+D_{2}\right)\)

Solving for the Conversion Ratio in DCM

Equate the two expressions for \(I_{L}\), charge balance on the left and the waveshape on the right, and solve for \(D+D_{2}\) with \(K \equiv 2L/(RT_{s})\):

\(\displaystyle \qquad \frac{V}{R} = \left(V_{g}-V\right)\left(\frac{DT_{s}}{2L}\right)\left(D+D_{2}\right) \quad\Rightarrow\quad D+D_{2} = \frac{K}{D}\cdot\frac{V}{V_{g}-V} = \frac{K}{D}\cdot\frac{M}{1-M}\)

Substitute into \(M = D/(D+D_{2})\) from volt-second balance. \(D_{2}\) is gone, and \(M\) is in known quantities:

\(\displaystyle \qquad M = \frac{D}{D+D_{2}} = \frac{D^{2}}{K}\cdot\frac{1-M}{M} \quad\Rightarrow\quad KM^{2} + D^{2}M - D^{2} = 0\)

Solve the quadratic; its positive root is the conversion ratio in DCM:

\(\displaystyle \qquad M = \frac{V}{V_{g}} = \frac{2}{1+\sqrt{1+\dfrac{4K}{D^{2}}}} = \frac{2}{1+\sqrt{1+\dfrac{8L}{D^{2}RT_{s}}}}\)

The Conversion Ratio in DCM

\(\displaystyle M = \frac{2}{1+\sqrt{1+\dfrac{4K}{D^{2}}}}, \qquad K = \frac{2L}{RT_{s}}\)

  • \(K\) compares the inductor to the load. Small \(K\) (a light load, a small \(L\)) is deep DCM: \(M\) runs well above \(D\), and \(V \to V_{g}\) long before \(D \to 1\).
  • Each curve rejoins the CCM line \(M = D\) once the converter is back in CCM; for \(K \ge 1\) it never leaves it. Why? Next slide.

Where the CCM/DCM Boundary Lies

DCM when \(I_{L} < \Delta i_{L}/2\). Evaluate both sides in CCM, where \(V = DV_{g}\):

\(\displaystyle I_{L} = \frac{DV_{g}}{R}, \qquad \frac{\Delta i_{L}}{2} = \frac{\left(V_{g}-V\right)DT_{s}}{2L} = \frac{V_{g}D\left(1-D\right)T_{s}}{2L}\)

\(\displaystyle \frac{DV_{g}}{R} < \frac{V_{g}D\left(1-D\right)T_{s}}{2L} \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad K = \frac{2L}{RT_{s}} < 1-D \equiv K_{crit}(D)\)

  • DCM for \(K < 1-D\), CCM for \(K > 1-D\): the boundary moves with \(D\), and a buck enters DCM at small \(D\) first.
  • \(K_{crit} \le 1\) for every \(D\). So \(K \ge 1\) (a large \(L\), a heavy load) keeps \(I_{L} \ge \Delta i_{L}/2\) at any duty ratio: never DCM.
